content: The evidence regarding the impact of mass drug administration (MDA) on the incidence of Plasmodium falciparum clinical malaria is highly uncertain. Specifically, the risk difference (RD) was estimated at -6 cases per 1,000 person-years (p-y), with a 95% confidence interval (CI) ranging from -9 to 0 cases per 1,000 p-y, based on four cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) with very low-certainty evidence. In terms of long-term benefits, 12–24 months after the last round of MDA, the evidence remains very uncertain regarding its effect on the prevalence of P. falciparum. The RD was -21 cases per 1,000 persons, with a 95% CI of -30 to 31 cases per 1,000 persons, based on one cRCT with very low-certainty evidence. However, MDA may reduce the incidence of P. falciparum clinical malaria, with an RD of -4 cases per 1,000 p-y (95% CI: 14 to 34 cases per 1,000 p-y), based on one cRCT with low-certainty evidence. Regarding serious adverse events, within 0–3 months of MDA, it is likely that MDA has little to no effect on serious adverse events, with an RD of 1 per 1,000 persons (95% CI: 0 to 11 per 1,000 persons), based on one cRCT with moderate-certainty evidence. Between 4–12 months, MDA may slightly increase serious adverse events, with an RD of 2 per 1,000 persons (95% CI: -1 to 8 per 1,000 persons), based on one cRCT with moderate-certainty evidence. The rate of serious adverse events per 1,000 doses of antimalarial medicine was estimated at 0.3, based on four cRCTs, though this was not graded due to the lack of comparator arm data. For general adverse events, the evidence is very uncertain about the effect of MDA within 1–3 months, with an RD of 300 per 1,000 persons (95% CI: -43 to 1,937 per 1,000 persons), based on one cRCT with very low-certainty evidence. The rate of adverse events per 1,000 doses of antimalarial medicine was estimated at 6, based on four cRCTs, though this was not graded due to the lack of comparator arm data. Concerning artemisinin resistance markers (PfKelch13), the evidence is very uncertain about the effect of MDA on these markers among P. falciparum infections within 1–3 months after the last round. The RD was -109 per 1,000 persons (95% CI: -334 to 310 per 1,000 persons), based on one cRCT with very low-certainty evidence. However, MDA may reduce the proportion of artemisinin resistance markers among all participants, with an RD of -56 per 1,000 persons (95% CI: -61 to -45 per 1,000 persons), based on one cRCT with low-certainty evidence. Between 4–12 months, the evidence remains very uncertain about the effect of MDA on the proportion of infections with artemisinin resistance markers among P. falciparum infections, with an RD of 98 per 1,000 persons (95% CI: -104 to 372 per 1,000 persons), based on one cRCT with very low-certainty evidence. However, MDA may reduce the proportion of artemisinin resistance markers among all participants, with an RD of -15 per 1,000 persons (95% CI: -21 to -4 per 1,000 persons), based on one cRCT with low-certainty evidence. At 12–24 months, the evidence remains very uncertain about the effect of MDA on the proportion of infections with artemisinin resistance markers among P. falciparum infections, with an RD of 50 per 1,000 persons (95% CI: -129 to 286 per 1,000 persons), based on one cRCT with very low-certainty evidence. However, MDA may reduce the proportion of artemisinin resistance markers among all participants, with an RD of -9 per 1,000 persons (95% CI: -15 to 3 per 1,000 persons), based on one cRCT with low-certainty evidence. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) noted challenges in assessing the effect of MDA on P. falciparum in very low to low transmission settings due to the limited number of studies and the overall low certainty of the evidence. The GDG judged the desirable effects of MDA to be moderate and the undesirable effects to be small. They concluded that the balance of effects probably favors MDA in areas of very low to low transmission, though concerns remain about the sustainability of impact if only one or two rounds are conducted. The overall certainty of the evidence was judged to be low. No studies were identified regarding preferences and values, and the GDG acknowledged potential variability in these factors. The GDG also noted that MDA could exacerbate inequity if not implemented appropriately or if the effects are only temporary. However, if MDA contributes to the elimination of P. falciparum, it could improve equity. The acceptability of MDA was judged to vary depending on whether community and individual concerns were addressed during intervention design. Previous experiences with MDA, whether positive or negative, were also considered likely to influence acceptance. The feasibility of implementing MDA was judged to vary depending on population size, with smaller populations and island communities being more feasible. Barriers to implementation included residents’ absence, seasonal mobility, and challenges in determining optimal timing due to weather, agricultural activities, religious events, and policy changes. The GDG concluded that a conditional recommendation for MDA in very low to low transmission settings should be issued, given the moderate-certainty evidence for short-term benefits, variability in acceptability and feasibility, and large resource requirements. Further research is needed to assess the impact and potential harms of MDA, including resistance to antimalarial medicines, disaggregated by sex, age, and socioeconomic status. Studies should also determine the optimal timing, number of rounds, and minimum effective coverage of MDA, as well as its feasibility and acceptability in elimination programs. Approaches to improve adherence and the potential role of single, low-dose primaquine should also be investigated. In moderate to high transmission settings, MDA is not recommended due to a lack of evidence for shortor long-term effects on P. falciparum transmission.
